en: I am free after three if you want to discuss.
tamil: நீங்க பேசணும்னா மூணு மணிக்கு மேல நான் ஃப்ரீ.
context: Offering a time to a colleague for a talk.
explain: 'If you want to' makes the offer flexible and polite.
usage: Use it with a teammate who needs a talk with you during a busy day.
leelaQ: When are you free to talk in the day?
answer: I am usually free in the afternoon after lunch.

en: I'm going to talk to my manager about the deadline.
tamil: டெட்லைனைப் பத்தி என் மேனேஜர்கிட்ட பேசப் போறேன்.
context: Saying what you plan to do about a tight deadline.
explain: 'Going to' shows a plan you have already decided to follow.
usage: Use it with a teammate when you have a plan to raise a problem with your boss.
leelaQ: Who will you talk to if a deadline is too tight?
answer: I am going to talk to my manager and ask for more time.

en: Should I add you to this email?
tamil: இந்த மின்னஞ்சல்ல உங்களையும் சேர்க்கணுமா?
context: Checking if a colleague should be in the mail loop.
explain: 'Should I' asks for advice or permission about your own action.
usage: Use it at work when you are not sure who should receive a message.
leelaQ: Who do you add in your office emails?
answer: I add my manager and the team members who need to know.

en: Is the client joining the call?
tamil: கிளையன்ட் காலுக்கு வர்றாரா?
context: Asking before a meeting begins.
explain: 'Is joining' can talk about a plan for the near future.
usage: Use it just before an online meeting when you are not sure who will attend.
leelaQ: Who usually joins your online meetings?
answer: Our team members and sometimes the client join them.

en: Our manager is travelling, so the meeting is online.
tamil: எங்க மேனேஜர் பயணத்துல இருக்காரு, அதனால மீட்டிங் ஆன்லைன்ல.
context: Explaining why the meeting is not in the office.
explain: 'So' joins a reason with a result.
usage: Use it when a teammate asks why the meeting is held online.
leelaQ: Do you prefer online or office meetings?
answer: I prefer office meetings because it is easy to talk face to face.

en: My colleague covered for me when I was sick.
tamil: நான் உடம்பு சரியில்லாம இருந்தப்போ என் கொலீக் என் வேலையை பாத்துக்கிட்டாரு.
context: Thanking a teammate who helped you.
explain: 'Covered for me' means did my work while I was away.
usage: Use it to thank a colleague or to tell a manager how teammates support each other.
leelaQ: Who helps you at work when you are away?
answer: My teammate takes care of my tasks when I am on leave.

en: We have not received the client's reply yet.
tamil: கிளையன்ட்டோட பதில் இன்னும் வரலை.
context: Updating a manager on a pending reply.
explain: 'Have not ... yet' means something is still pending.
usage: Use it when your manager asks if the client has answered.
leelaQ: What do you do when a client does not reply?
answer: I send a reminder and then I call them.

en: Has everyone received the agenda?
tamil: எல்லாருக்கும் அஜெண்டா வந்துடுச்சா?
context: Checking before a meeting starts.
explain: 'Has everyone' takes a singular verb. An agenda is a list of topics for a meeting.
usage: Use it as an organiser before a meeting to make sure people are ready.
leelaQ: What does a good meeting agenda have?
answer: It has the topics, the time and the names of the speakers.

en: I wrote down all the points from the meeting.
tamil: மீட்டிங்ல இருந்த எல்லா பாயின்ட்களையும் எழுதி வச்சிருக்கேன்.
context: Telling a colleague you have the meeting notes.
explain: 'Wrote down' is the past of 'write down'. It means to make a written note.
usage: Use it when a teammate missed the meeting and wants the details.
leelaQ: Do you take notes in meetings?
answer: Yes, I write the main points in my notebook.

en: You should share your ideas in the meeting.
tamil: மீட்டிங்ல உங்க ஐடியாக்களை சொல்லணும்.
context: Encouraging a shy teammate to speak up.
explain: 'Should' is used to give friendly advice.
usage: Use it to encourage a junior colleague who stays quiet in meetings.
leelaQ: Do you share your ideas in meetings?
answer: Yes, I share my ideas when I feel confident about them.

en: Your feedback helped me a lot.
tamil: உங்க ஃபீட்பேக் எனக்கு ரொம்ப உதவியா இருந்துச்சு.
context: Thanking a senior for useful comments.
explain: 'Helped me a lot' is a warm way to thank someone for advice.
usage: Use it after a manager or senior gives you good feedback on your work.
leelaQ: Who gave you useful feedback recently?
answer: My team lead gave me good feedback on my last report.

en: We are going to launch the update next week.
tamil: நாங்க அடுத்த வாரம் அப்டேட்டை வெளியிடப் போறோம்.
context: Announcing a plan to the whole team.
explain: 'Going to' is good for planned events. 'Launch' means to start something new.
usage: Use it when you tell the team or a client about a planned release.
leelaQ: What is your team planning for next week?
answer: We are going to test the new feature and share it.

en: We have a new target for this month.
tamil: இந்த மாசத்துக்கு எங்களுக்கு ஒரு புது டார்கெட் இருக்கு.
context: Telling the team about a new goal.
explain: 'Have' is used here for something that belongs to the team.
usage: Use it when a manager shares monthly goals with the team.
leelaQ: What target do you have this month?
answer: I have to finish three tasks before the end of the month.

en: I could finish early because the team helped.
tamil: டீம் உதவுனதால நான் சீக்கிரம் முடிக்க முடிஞ்சது.
context: Crediting your teammates for a quick finish.
explain: 'Could' is used here for ability in the past. 'Because' gives the reason.
usage: Use it to give credit to your team when your manager praises you.
leelaQ: How does teamwork help you at work?
answer: It helps me finish my tasks faster and learn new things.

en: Our team lead sends the daily summary at six.
tamil: எங்க டீம் லீட் தினமும் ஆறு மணிக்கு சுருக்கத்தை அனுப்புவாரு.
context: Explaining the daily routine to a new joiner.
explain: The simple present is used for fixed daily routines. 'Sends' takes an 's' after 'lead'.
usage: Use it to explain office routines to a new person in your team.
leelaQ: What daily reports do you send or receive?
answer: I get a daily summary from my team lead in the evening.

en: I have attached the document to this email.
tamil: இந்த மின்னஞ்சல்ல டாக்குமென்ட்டை இணைச்சிருக்கேன்.
context: Writing the first lines of an email with a file.
explain: 'Have attached' is the usual phrase in emails. It tells the reader to check the file.
usage: Use it in an email when you send a file along with your message.
leelaQ: What do you write when you send a file by email?
answer: I write that I have attached the file and ask them to check it.

en: He explained the problem very clearly.
tamil: அவர் பிரச்சனையை ரொம்ப தெளிவா விளக்குனாரு.
context: Praising a colleague after a meeting.
explain: 'Clearly' is an adverb that tells how he explained.
usage: Use it to praise a teammate in front of others or to your manager.
leelaQ: Can you explain your work clearly to others?
answer: Yes, I use simple words and give small examples.

en: Could you explain that point again?
tamil: அந்த பாயின்ட்டை ஒருமுறை திரும்ப விளக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a speaker to repeat politely.
explain: 'Could you' sounds more polite than 'can you'.
usage: Use it in a meeting or a call when you missed a detail.
leelaQ: How do you ask someone to repeat something?
answer: I say could you explain that again, please.

en: The meeting has been moved to four o'clock.
tamil: மீட்டிங்கை நாலு மணிக்கு மாத்திட்டாங்க.
context: Telling a colleague about a new meeting time.
explain: 'Has been moved' shows a change that is already done. It is common in office updates.
usage: Use it when you tell your team that a meeting time has changed.
leelaQ: What do you say when a meeting time changes?
answer: I tell my team that the meeting has been moved to a new time.

en: We have finished almost sixty percent of the work.
tamil: கிட்டத்தட்ட அறுபது சதவீத வேலையை முடிச்சிட்டோம்.
context: Giving a progress update to a manager.
explain: 'Almost' means nearly. 'Have finished' links the work done to the present.
usage: Use it when your manager asks how much work is complete.
leelaQ: How much of your work is finished today?
answer: I have finished about half of my tasks.

en: I agree with you, but I have one small concern.
tamil: நீங்க சொல்றது சரிதான், ஆனா எனக்கு ஒரு சின்ன கவலை இருக்கு.
context: Politely raising a doubt in a discussion.
explain: Start with 'I agree' and then use 'but' to add your doubt. It sounds polite.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you accept an idea but want to raise a point.
leelaQ: How do you raise a doubt politely in a meeting?
answer: I say I agree first, and then I explain my small concern.

en: Did the manager approve my leave?
tamil: மேனேஜர் என் லீவை அங்கீகரிச்சாரா?
context: Asking a teammate or HR about leave status.
explain: 'Approve' means to officially say yes to something.
usage: Use it with HR or a colleague when you are waiting for leave approval.
leelaQ: When do you apply for leave in your company?
answer: I apply at least a week before I need the leave.

en: The feedback was honest, and I accepted it.
tamil: ஃபீட்பேக் நேர்மையா இருந்துச்சு, நானும் அதை ஏத்துக்கிட்டேன்.
context: Telling a friend how you took criticism.
explain: 'And' joins two past actions. 'Accepted' means took it without anger.
usage: Use it to show a mature attitude when you talk about criticism.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you get feedback?
answer: I feel a little nervous, but I try to learn from it.

en: I will send you the updated file by evening.
tamil: சாயங்காலத்துக்குள்ள அப்டேட் பண்ண ஃபைலை அனுப்பிடறேன்.
context: Promising a colleague a revised document.
explain: 'Will' is used for a promise. 'By evening' sets a clear deadline.
usage: Use it with a teammate who is waiting for your work.
leelaQ: When do you usually send your reports to your manager?
answer: I usually send them before lunch so my manager can check them.

en: What time is the review call?
tamil: ரிவியூ கால் எத்தனை மணிக்கு?
context: Asking a teammate about a meeting time.
explain: A short and common question for schedules.
usage: Use it with a colleague when you forgot the time of a meeting.
leelaQ: What time does your office day start?
answer: It starts at nine thirty in the morning.
